chapter_text:
CHAPTER 29 — NATURAL ENVIRONMENT

Introduction

Every living organism — a tiny bacterium, a blade of grass, a fish, a tiger or a human being — survives by interacting continuously with its surroundings. These surroundings, taken together, make up the ENVIRONMENT. The environment supplies the air we breathe, the water we drink, the food we eat and the space in which we live. This chapter studies the natural environment: what it is made of, how living and non-living parts interact in units called ecosystems, how food and energy flow through them, how essential materials are recycled, and why protecting the ozone layer and biodiversity is essential for maintaining the balance of nature.

29.1 ENVIRONMENT AND ITS COMPONENTS

The ENVIRONMENT is the sum total of all the surroundings — living and non-living — of an organism. It has two kinds of components:
 - BIOTIC components: all the living things — plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and other micro-organisms.
 - ABIOTIC components: all the non-living physical and chemical factors — sunlight, temperature, air, water, soil, minerals, humidity and pH.
The biotic and abiotic components are not isolated; they constantly interact. Plants take minerals and water from the soil and energy from the sun; animals depend on plants; and when organisms die, decomposers return their materials to the soil. These interactions tie the living and non-living worlds into functional units.

29.2 ECOSYSTEM

An ECOSYSTEM is a functional unit of nature in which living organisms (the biotic community) interact among themselves and with their non-living (abiotic) surroundings, exchanging materials and energy. The term was coined by A. G. Tansley in 1935. A pond, a forest, a grassland, a desert and even a drop of water can each be regarded as an ecosystem.

Types of ecosystems:
 - NATURAL ecosystems form and run on their own, without human control. Examples: a FOREST, a POND or lake, a GRASSLAND, a desert, a river and the ocean. Natural ecosystems are further divided into TERRESTRIAL (land-based, e.g. forest, grassland, desert) and AQUATIC (water-based, e.g. pond, lake, river, sea).
 - ARTIFICIAL (man-made) ecosystems are created and maintained by humans. Examples: an AQUARIUM, a CROP FIELD (agro-ecosystem), a garden and a zoo. They need human inputs such as fertilisers, water and care, and would not survive on their own for long.
Every ecosystem, natural or artificial, has a STRUCTURE (its components and their arrangement) and a FUNCTION (the flow of energy and the cycling of nutrients through it).

29.3 COMPONENTS OF AN ECOSYSTEM

The biotic part of an ecosystem is organised by the way organisms obtain their food:

(a) PRODUCERS (autotrophs): green plants, algae and some bacteria that make their own food by PHOTOSYNTHESIS, using sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to build glucose. Because they trap solar energy and bring it into the living world, producers form the base of every ecosystem.

(b) CONSUMERS (heterotrophs): organisms that cannot make their own food and so feed on other organisms. They are grouped by what they eat:
   - HERBIVORES (primary consumers) eat only plants — e.g. cow, deer, grasshopper, rabbit.
   - CARNIVORES (secondary or higher consumers) eat other animals — e.g. frog, snake, lion, hawk. A carnivore that eats a herbivore is a secondary consumer; one that eats another carnivore is a tertiary consumer.
   - OMNIVORES eat both plants and animals — e.g. humans, crow, bear.

(c) DECOMPOSERS (saprotrophs / micro-consumers): bacteria and fungi that break down the dead bodies and wastes of plants and animals into simple substances. They release minerals back into the soil, water and air, where producers can use them again. Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up and nutrients would be locked away forever.

The ABIOTIC components — sunlight, air (CO2, O2), water, soil, minerals and temperature — supply the raw materials and the energy that the biotic community depends upon.

29.4 FOOD CHAIN AND FOOD WEB

FOOD CHAIN: A food chain is the sequence of organisms through which food (and the energy in it) passes, each organism eating the one before it and being eaten by the one after it. A simple grassland food chain is:
   Grass -> Grasshopper -> Frog -> Snake -> Hawk.
Here grass is the producer; the grasshopper is the primary consumer (herbivore); the frog, snake and hawk are successive carnivores. Energy and nutrients flow in ONE direction along the chain. A pond food chain might be: Phytoplankton -> Zooplankton -> Small fish -> Big fish.

TROPHIC LEVELS: Each step or 'feeding level' in a food chain is called a TROPHIC LEVEL. Producers occupy the first trophic level, herbivores the second, primary carnivores the third, and so on. The trophic level tells us the position of an organism in the flow of energy.

FOOD WEB: In nature, organisms rarely eat only one kind of food, and a single organism is usually eaten by several others. So food chains are interconnected to form a FOOD WEB — a network of many interlinked food chains in an ecosystem. For example, a hawk may eat both snakes and birds, and a frog may be eaten by both snakes and hawks. Food webs make an ecosystem more STABLE: if one species declines, predators can switch to alternative prey, so the whole system is less likely to collapse.

29.5 FLOW OF ENERGY IN AN ECOSYSTEM

The ultimate source of energy for almost all ecosystems is the SUN. Green plants capture only a small fraction of the sunlight falling on them and convert it into chemical energy (food) by photosynthesis. This energy then flows from producers to consumers along food chains.

The flow of energy is UNIDIRECTIONAL — it moves from the sun to producers to consumers and is finally lost as heat; it does NOT cycle back. (Nutrients, in contrast, are recycled.)

THE 10 PER CENT LAW (Lindeman's law): When energy passes from one trophic level to the next, only about 10 per cent of the energy is stored in the body of the organism at the higher level and is available to the next level. The remaining ~90 per cent is used up in the organism's life processes (respiration, movement, maintaining body heat) and lost to the surroundings as heat. So if producers store 1000 units of energy, herbivores get about 100 units, primary carnivores about 10 units, and the next level only about 1 unit.

WHY FOOD CHAINS ARE SHORT: Because so much energy (about 90 per cent) is lost at every step, very little is left after three or four transfers. There is simply not enough energy to support many higher trophic levels. This is why most food chains have only 3 to 5 links.

29.6 ECOLOGICAL PYRAMIDS

The relationships between successive trophic levels can be shown as ECOLOGICAL PYRAMIDS — graphical figures, broad at the base (producers) and narrowing towards the top. There are three kinds:
 - PYRAMID OF NUMBERS: shows the number of organisms at each trophic level. Usually upright (many grass plants, fewer herbivores, still fewer carnivores), but it can be inverted — for example one large tree supports many insects.
 - PYRAMID OF BIOMASS: shows the total dry weight (biomass) of organisms at each level. In most land ecosystems it is upright; in some aquatic systems it can be inverted.
 - PYRAMID OF ENERGY: shows the amount of energy at each trophic level. Because of the 10 per cent law, the energy pyramid is ALWAYS UPRIGHT — energy can only decrease as we move up.

29.7 BIOGEOCHEMICAL CYCLES

Unlike energy, the chemical elements that make up living matter are limited in quantity and so must be used again and again. The cyclic movement of nutrient elements between the living organisms and the non-living environment is called a BIOGEOCHEMICAL CYCLE ('bio' = living, 'geo' = earth). The main cycles are:

(a) CARBON CYCLE: Carbon moves between the atmosphere (as CO2), living organisms and the earth. Plants take in CO2 during photosynthesis and fix it into food. Respiration by plants and animals, decay of dead matter, and the burning (combustion) of wood and fossil fuels return CO2 to the air.

(b) NITROGEN CYCLE: The air is about 78% nitrogen gas (N2), but most organisms cannot use it directly. NITROGEN FIXATION — by lightning and by nitrogen-fixing bacteria (e.g. Rhizobium in the roots of legumes) — converts N2 into nitrates that plants can absorb. Animals get nitrogen by eating plants. Decomposers release nitrogen from dead matter (ammonification), and DENITRIFYING bacteria return free nitrogen gas to the atmosphere.

(c) WATER CYCLE (hydrological cycle): Water EVAPORATES from oceans, rivers and lakes (and TRANSPIRES from plants) into the air, CONDENSES to form clouds, falls back as PRECIPITATION (rain, snow), and flows over and through the land back to the sea — an endless cycle driven by the sun.

(d) OXYGEN CYCLE: Oxygen is released into the air by green plants during photosynthesis and is used up by all organisms during respiration and by combustion. Photosynthesis and respiration thus keep the levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere roughly balanced.

29.8 THE OZONE LAYER

High up in the stratosphere lies a layer rich in OZONE (O3). This OZONE LAYER acts as a protective shield: it absorbs most of the harmful ULTRAVIOLET (UV) radiation coming from the sun. UV rays can cause skin cancer, cataracts (eye damage) and a weakened immune system in humans, and can damage crops and aquatic life. By filtering out UV, the ozone layer makes life on land possible.

OZONE DEPLETION: Certain man-made chemicals, especially CHLOROFLUOROCARBONS (CFCs) used in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays, rise into the stratosphere and destroy ozone molecules. This thinning of the ozone layer — most marked over Antarctica, where it is called the 'OZONE HOLE' — lets more UV reach the ground. The international Montreal Protocol (1987) banned CFCs to allow the ozone layer to recover.

29.9 BALANCE IN NATURE (ECOLOGICAL BALANCE)

In an undisturbed ecosystem, the numbers of producers, consumers and decomposers, and the cycling of materials, stay in a steady state called ECOLOGICAL BALANCE. Food webs, energy flow and biogeochemical cycles together maintain this balance. Human activities — deforestation, pollution, over-hunting, the introduction of foreign species and the release of CFCs and greenhouse gases — can upset the balance, leading to problems such as extinction of species, global warming and ozone depletion.

29.10 BIODIVERSITY AND ITS IMPORTANCE

BIODIVERSITY (biological diversity) is the variety of all living organisms — the different species of plants, animals and micro-organisms — found in a region. India is one of the world's 'mega-diverse' countries. Biodiversity is important because it keeps ecosystems stable and resilient, provides food, medicines, timber, fibres and other resources, maintains the cycles of nature (clean air, water and fertile soil), and has great aesthetic and cultural value. Loss of biodiversity weakens ecosystems and reduces nature's ability to recover from disturbance, so its CONSERVATION (through national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves) is essential.

SUMMARY

- The environment is the sum of an organism's biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) surroundings.
- An ecosystem is a functional unit where the biotic community interacts with the abiotic environment; it may be natural (forest, pond, grassland) or artificial (aquarium, crop field).
- Biotic components are producers (autotrophs), consumers (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores) and decomposers.
- A food chain is a one-way feeding sequence; interconnected food chains form a food web; each feeding step is a trophic level.
- Energy flows one way from the sun through producers to consumers; only about 10 per cent passes to the next level (10% law), which is why food chains are short.
- Ecological pyramids (of number, biomass, energy) depict trophic structure; the energy pyramid is always upright.
- Nutrients are recycled through biogeochemical cycles — carbon, nitrogen, water and oxygen cycles.
- The ozone layer shields the earth from UV radiation; CFCs cause ozone depletion (the 'ozone hole').
- Ecological balance and biodiversity must be conserved for ecosystems to remain healthy and self-sustaining.

learning_outcomes.description: Define environment and ecosystem, distinguish biotic from abiotic components, and classify ecosystems as natural or artificial with examples.
Identify the biotic components of an ecosystem (producers, consumers, decomposers) and classify consumers as herbivores, carnivores and omnivores.
Construct and interpret food chains and food webs, and assign organisms to their correct trophic levels.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Flow of Energy and Ecological Pyramids
learning_outcomes.description: Explain the unidirectional flow of energy and the 10 per cent law, and use it to explain why food chains are short and why the energy pyramid is always upright.
Describe the carbon, nitrogen, water and oxygen biogeochemical cycles and explain why nutrients are recycled while energy is not.
Explain the importance of the ozone layer, the cause and effects of ozone depletion, and the meaning of ecological balance and biodiversity conservation.
Predict the effect on a food web of the removal or decline of one species and explain how food webs lend stability to ecosystems.
Evaluate how human activities disturb ecological balance and the ozone layer, and justify measures taken to conserve biodiversity and the environment.

chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) summary for Lesson 29. It covers the environment and its biotic and abiotic components, ecosystems and their structure, food chains and food webs, the flow of energy and ecological pyramids, the biogeochemical cycles, and the importance of the ozone layer, ecological balance and biodiversity.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Natural Environment (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) Worksheet for Lesson 29 (Natural Environment). Attempt all questions. Draw labelled diagrams of food chains and cycles where helpful.

questions.question: Define an ecosystem. Name two natural and two artificial ecosystems.
questions.answer:
An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature in which living organisms (the biotic community) interact among themselves and with their non-living (abiotic) surroundings, exchanging energy and materials.
Natural ecosystems: a forest and a pond (also grassland, desert, river, ocean).
Artificial (man-made) ecosystems: an aquarium and a crop field (also a garden or zoo).
questions.explanation: Definition plus correct classification with examples.

questions.question: Distinguish between biotic and abiotic components of the environment, giving two examples of each.
questions.answer:
Biotic components are the LIVING parts of the environment — examples: plants and animals (also fungi, bacteria).
Abiotic components are the NON-LIVING physical and chemical factors — examples: sunlight and water (also air, soil, temperature, minerals).
The biotic and abiotic components constantly interact: organisms take materials and energy from the abiotic surroundings and return them when they die.
questions.explanation: Living vs non-living distinction with examples.

questions.question: Who are decomposers? Why are they important in an ecosystem?
questions.answer:
Decomposers are micro-organisms — mainly bacteria and fungi — that break down the dead bodies and wastes of plants and animals into simple substances.
They are important because they return minerals and nutrients to the soil, water and air, where producers can use them again. Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up and nutrients would remain locked in dead bodies, so the cycling of materials would stop.
questions.explanation: Definition plus their role in nutrient recycling.

questions.question: Construct a food chain found in a grassland and label the trophic level of each organism.
questions.answer:
A grassland food chain: Grass -> Grasshopper -> Frog -> Snake -> Hawk.
Trophic levels:
- Grass = producer (first trophic level)
- Grasshopper = primary consumer / herbivore (second level)
- Frog = secondary consumer / carnivore (third level)
- Snake = tertiary consumer / carnivore (fourth level)
- Hawk = top carnivore (fifth level).
Energy and nutrients flow in one direction along the chain.
questions.explanation: Correct chain with trophic levels assigned.

questions.question: Explain the flow of energy in an ecosystem. State the 10 per cent law and use it to explain why food chains are short.
questions.answer:
The sun is the ultimate source of energy for almost all ecosystems. Green plants (producers) capture a small fraction of sunlight and convert it into chemical energy (food) by photosynthesis. This energy then flows from producers to herbivores to carnivores along food chains.
The flow of energy is UNIDIRECTIONAL — it moves from the sun to producers to consumers and is finally lost as heat; it does not return.
10 PER CENT LAW: When energy passes from one trophic level to the next, only about 10% of the energy is stored in the body of the organism at the higher level and is available to the next level. The remaining ~90% is used up in life processes (respiration, movement) and lost as heat.
WHY FOOD CHAINS ARE SHORT: Since about 90% of the energy is lost at each step, very little energy is left after three or four transfers. There is not enough energy to support many higher levels, so most food chains have only 3 to 5 links.
questions.explanation: Unidirectional flow, 10% law and its consequence for chain length.

questions.question: Name the three types of ecological pyramids. Which one is always upright and why?
questions.answer:
The three ecological pyramids are the pyramid of NUMBERS, the pyramid of BIOMASS and the pyramid of ENERGY.
The pyramid of ENERGY is always upright. This is because of the 10 per cent law: energy decreases at every higher trophic level (only ~10% is passed on), so the amount of energy can never increase as we go up. Pyramids of number and biomass can sometimes be inverted, but the energy pyramid never is.
questions.explanation: Names plus the 10% reasoning for the upright energy pyramid.

questions.question: Describe the nitrogen cycle in brief.
questions.answer:
The air is about 78% nitrogen gas (N2), but most organisms cannot use it directly.
- NITROGEN FIXATION: lightning and nitrogen-fixing bacteria (e.g. Rhizobium in the root nodules of legumes) convert N2 into nitrates that plants can absorb.
- Plants use the nitrates to build proteins; animals get nitrogen by eating plants.
- AMMONIFICATION: decomposers break down dead matter and release nitrogen compounds back into the soil.
- DENITRIFICATION: denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back to free nitrogen gas, returning it to the atmosphere.
Thus nitrogen cycles between the air, the soil and living organisms.

questions.question: What is the ozone layer? Why is it important and what causes its depletion?
questions.answer:
The ozone layer is a layer rich in ozone (O3) in the stratosphere.
Importance: it absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun. UV rays can cause skin cancer, cataracts and weakened immunity in humans and can damage crops and aquatic life. By filtering out UV, the ozone layer makes life on land possible.
Depletion: man-made chemicals, especially chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) from refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosols, rise into the stratosphere and destroy ozone molecules. This thinning — most marked over Antarctica — is called the ozone hole. The Montreal Protocol (1987) banned CFCs to help the layer recover.
questions.explanation: Definition, protective role, and CFCs as the cause of depletion.

questions.question: If all the frogs in the food web Grass -> Grasshopper -> Frog -> Snake -> Hawk were removed, what would happen? Explain.
questions.answer:
Removing the frogs disturbs the food web in both directions:
- Grasshoppers (the frog's prey) would lose a predator, so their numbers would increase. The larger grasshopper population would eat more grass, possibly reducing the producers.
- Snakes (which feed on frogs) would lose a food source. If they cannot switch to other prey, snake numbers would fall, which in turn affects the hawks.
If the food web has alternative links (e.g. snakes can eat other animals), the effect is cushioned — this shows why food webs make an ecosystem more stable than a single food chain.
questions.explanation: Effect propagates up and down the web; food-web links add stability.

questions.question: What is biodiversity? Give two reasons why its conservation is important.
questions.answer:
Biodiversity (biological diversity) is the variety of all living organisms — the different species of plants, animals and micro-organisms — found in a region.
Two reasons for conserving it:
1. It keeps ecosystems stable and resilient and maintains the natural cycles (clean air, water, fertile soil) that life depends on.
2. It provides resources such as food, medicines, timber and fibres, and has aesthetic and cultural value.
Conservation is done through national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves.
questions.explanation: Definition plus two valid reasons for conservation.

A forest is an artificial ecosystem.
questions.explanation: A forest is a natural ecosystem.

questions.question: Green plants are producers in an ecosystem.
Decomposers build up complex food from simple substances.
questions.explanation: Decomposers break complex dead matter into simple substances.

questions.question: A food web is more stable than a single food chain.
Energy flow in an ecosystem is unidirectional.
questions.explanation: Energy is finally lost as heat.

questions.question: About 90 per cent of energy is passed from one trophic level to the next.
questions.explanation: Only about 10% is passed on; ~90% is lost.

questions.question: Nutrients are recycled in an ecosystem while energy is not.
questions.explanation: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

questions.question: The ozone layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
questions.explanation: It shields life on earth from UV.

questions.question: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) help to build up the ozone layer.
The non-living components of the environment are called ____ components.
An ____ is a functional unit where organisms interact with their non-living surroundings.
An aquarium is an example of a/an ____ ecosystem.
Organisms that make their own food are called ____.
Animals that eat only plants are called ____.
Bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter are called ____.
Each feeding step in a food chain is called a ____ level.
A network of interconnected food chains is called a ____.
The ultimate source of energy for an ecosystem is the ____.
According to the ____ law, only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level.
Plants absorb ____ gas during photosynthesis.
The bacterium ____ found in legume root nodules fixes nitrogen.
The chemical formula of ozone is ____.
The ozone layer protects the earth from harmful ____ radiation.
Ozone depletion is mainly caused by chemicals called ____.
What is meant by the environment?
questions.answer: The environment is the sum total of all the surroundings — both living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) — of an organism. It supplies the air, water, food, and space that organisms need to live, and its biotic and abiotic parts constantly interact.
questions.explanation: Definition with biotic and abiotic parts.

questions.question: Give two examples each of biotic and abiotic components.
questions.answer:
Biotic (living) components: plants and animals (also fungi, bacteria).
Abiotic (non-living) components: sunlight and water (also air, soil, temperature, minerals).

questions.question: Differentiate between a natural and an artificial ecosystem with one example each.
questions.answer: A natural ecosystem forms and runs on its own without human control, e.g. a forest. An artificial (man-made) ecosystem is created and maintained by humans with regular inputs such as water and food, e.g. an aquarium. An artificial ecosystem would not survive long on its own.

questions.question: Name the two terrestrial and two aquatic natural ecosystems.
questions.answer:
Terrestrial (land-based) natural ecosystems: forest and grassland (also desert).
Aquatic (water-based) natural ecosystems: pond and river (also lake and ocean).

questions.question: Who are producers? Why are they called the base of the ecosystem?
questions.answer: Producers are autotrophs — green plants, algae and some bacteria — that make their own food by photosynthesis using sunlight, CO2 and water. They are the base of the ecosystem because they trap solar energy and bring it into the living world; all consumers depend, directly or indirectly, on producers for food and energy.
questions.explanation: Definition plus their role as energy entry point.

questions.question: Classify consumers into three types with one example of each.
questions.answer:
Consumers are classified by what they eat:
- Herbivores (primary consumers) eat only plants, e.g. cow or deer.
- Carnivores eat other animals, e.g. lion or snake.
- Omnivores eat both plants and animals, e.g. humans or crow.

questions.question: Why are decomposers essential for the cycling of nutrients?
questions.answer: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down the dead bodies and wastes of plants and animals into simple substances. They release minerals back into the soil, water and air, where producers can absorb and reuse them. Without decomposers, dead matter would accumulate and nutrients would stay locked in dead bodies, halting the nutrient cycle.
questions.explanation: Break down dead matter; recycle minerals.

questions.question: Distinguish between autotrophs and heterotrophs.
questions.answer: Autotrophs make their own food (e.g. green plants, by photosynthesis); they are the producers. Heterotrophs cannot make their own food and depend on other organisms for it; they are the consumers (and decomposers).

questions.question: What is a food chain? Give one example.
questions.answer: A food chain is a sequence of organisms through which food and the energy in it pass, each organism eating the one before it and being eaten by the one after it. Example: Grass -> Grasshopper -> Frog -> Snake -> Hawk.

questions.question: What is a trophic level? Name the trophic level of grass, deer and tiger in a food chain.
questions.answer: A trophic level is a feeding step or position of an organism in a food chain. In Grass -> Deer -> Tiger: grass is at the first trophic level (producer), deer at the second (herbivore/primary consumer), and tiger at the third (carnivore/secondary consumer).

questions.question: How does a food web differ from a food chain? Why is a food web more stable?
questions.answer: A food chain is a single, straight-line feeding sequence, whereas a food web is a network of many interconnected food chains. A food web is more stable because most organisms have several food sources and predators; if one species declines, predators can switch to alternative prey, so the whole ecosystem is less likely to collapse.
questions.explanation: Single line vs network; alternative links add stability.

questions.question: From the organisms grass, rabbit, fox and hawk, construct a food chain and identify the producer and the top carnivore.
questions.answer:
A food chain: Grass -> Rabbit -> Fox -> Hawk (or Grass -> Rabbit -> Hawk).
The producer is the grass (it makes its own food). The top carnivore is the hawk, which is not eaten by any other organism in the chain.
questions.explanation: Correct ordering; producer and top carnivore identified.

questions.question: State the 10 per cent law of energy flow.
questions.answer: The 10 per cent law (Lindeman's law) states that when energy passes from one trophic level to the next, only about 10 per cent of it is stored in the body of the organism at the higher level and is available to the next level; the remaining ~90 per cent is used in life processes and lost as heat.

questions.question: Why is the flow of energy in an ecosystem said to be unidirectional?
questions.answer: Energy enters the ecosystem from the sun, is fixed by producers, and then passes from producers to consumers along food chains. At each step a large part is lost as heat through respiration and other life processes. This lost heat cannot be reused by organisms, so energy moves only in one direction — from the sun through the trophic levels and finally out as heat — and never cycles back. (Nutrients, by contrast, are recycled.)

questions.question: If green plants in an ecosystem capture 5000 J of energy, how much is available to the primary carnivores? Show your reasoning.
questions.answer:
Using the 10 per cent law:
- Producers: 5000 J.
- Herbivores (primary consumers) get 10% of 5000 J = 500 J.
- Primary carnivores (secondary consumers) get 10% of 500 J = 50 J.
So about 50 J of energy is available to the primary carnivores.

questions.question: Name the three types of ecological pyramids and state which is always upright.
questions.answer: The three ecological pyramids are the pyramid of numbers, the pyramid of biomass and the pyramid of energy. The pyramid of energy is always upright, because energy can only decrease as we move up the trophic levels (10 per cent law).

questions.question: What is a biogeochemical cycle? Name any two.
questions.answer: A biogeochemical cycle is the cyclic movement of a nutrient element between living organisms and the non-living environment, so that the limited supply of the element can be used again and again. Two examples: the carbon cycle and the nitrogen cycle (also the water and oxygen cycles).

questions.question: Briefly describe the carbon cycle.
questions.answer: In the carbon cycle, carbon moves between the atmosphere (as CO2), living organisms and the earth. Plants absorb CO2 during photosynthesis and fix it into food. Respiration by plants and animals, the decay of dead matter by decomposers, and the burning (combustion) of wood and fossil fuels return CO2 to the atmosphere. Thus carbon is continuously recycled.
questions.explanation: CO2 uptake by photosynthesis; return by respiration, decay, combustion.

questions.question: Describe the water cycle in brief.
questions.answer: In the water (hydrological) cycle, water evaporates from oceans, rivers and lakes and transpires from plants into the air. The vapour condenses to form clouds and falls back to the earth as precipitation (rain or snow). The water then flows over and through the land back to the sea, and the cycle repeats. It is driven by the sun's heat.

questions.question: Explain why matter is recycled in an ecosystem but energy is not.
questions.answer: The chemical elements that make up living matter (carbon, nitrogen, etc.) are limited in quantity, so they must be used again and again; decomposers return them to the environment, where producers reuse them — hence matter cycles. Energy, however, is continuously supplied by the sun and is degraded to heat at each trophic level (respiration, life processes). This heat cannot be reused by organisms, so energy flows one way through the ecosystem and is finally lost; it is not recycled.
questions.explanation: Limited matter is recycled; energy degrades to unusable heat.

questions.question: What roles do photosynthesis and respiration play in the oxygen cycle?
questions.answer: In the oxygen cycle, green plants release oxygen into the air during photosynthesis, while all organisms use up oxygen during respiration (and combustion uses it too). Photosynthesis and respiration are opposite processes that together keep the levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere roughly balanced.
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis releases O2; respiration uses it.

questions.question: What is the ozone layer and why is it important?
questions.answer: The ozone layer is a layer rich in ozone (O3) in the stratosphere. It is important because it absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun. By filtering out UV — which can cause skin cancer, cataracts and weakened immunity, and can damage crops and aquatic life — the ozone layer makes life on land possible.

questions.question: What causes ozone depletion and what are its harmful effects?
questions.answer: Ozone depletion is caused mainly by man-made chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), used in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays. These rise into the stratosphere and destroy ozone molecules, thinning the ozone layer (the 'ozone hole', most marked over Antarctica). As a result, more UV radiation reaches the ground, increasing skin cancer, cataracts and immune problems in humans and harming crops and aquatic life.
questions.explanation: CFCs deplete ozone; more UV reaches earth.

questions.question: What is meant by ecological balance?
questions.answer: Ecological balance is the steady state of an undisturbed ecosystem, in which the numbers of producers, consumers and decomposers, and the cycling of materials, remain in equilibrium. It is maintained by food webs, energy flow and biogeochemical cycles.
questions.explanation: Steady state of an undisturbed ecosystem.

questions.question: List three human activities that disturb ecological balance.
questions.answer: Three human activities that disturb ecological balance are: (1) deforestation (cutting down forests); (2) pollution of air, water and soil; and (3) over-hunting of animals. Others include introducing foreign species and releasing CFCs and greenhouse gases. These activities can cause extinction of species, global warming and ozone depletion.

questions.question: What is biodiversity? Why should it be conserved?
questions.answer: Biodiversity is the variety of all living organisms — the different species of plants, animals and micro-organisms — in a region. It should be conserved because it keeps ecosystems stable and resilient, maintains nature's cycles, and provides food, medicines, timber and other resources, besides having aesthetic and cultural value.
questions.explanation: Variety of life; reasons for conservation.

questions.question: How can biodiversity be conserved? Mention two methods.
questions.answer: Biodiversity can be conserved by protecting natural habitats and species. Two methods: (1) setting up protected areas such as national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves; and (2) banning the hunting of endangered animals and controlling pollution and deforestation. Public awareness and afforestation also help.

questions.question: Why does the removal of one species from a food web affect many other organisms?
questions.answer: In a food web, each species is linked to several others as prey or predator. Removing one species therefore breaks several links: its prey may increase (losing a predator) and its predators may decline (losing a food source). These changes ripple through the connected chains, affecting many organisms. A food web with many alternative links can cushion such effects better than a single food chain.
questions.explanation: Interlinked feeding relationships spread the effect.

questions.question: In a food web, hawks eat both snakes and rats. If snakes disappear, what happens to the rats and the hawks?
questions.answer: If snakes disappear: (1) rats lose one of their predators (snakes), so the rat population would tend to increase; (2) hawks lose one food source (snakes) but can switch to eating more rats, so they may survive on the alternative prey. Because the hawk has an alternative food link (rats), the food web is more stable than a single chain would be.
questions.explanation: Prey of snakes rises; hawks switch to alternative prey.

questions.question: Arrange these organisms into a correct food chain: snake, grass, hawk, grasshopper, frog.
questions.answer:
The correct food chain is: Grass -> Grasshopper -> Frog -> Snake -> Hawk.
Grass is the producer, the grasshopper is the herbivore (primary consumer), and the frog, snake and hawk are successive carnivores, with the hawk as the top carnivore.
questions.explanation: Producer first, then consumers in feeding order.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A village pond contains water plants and algae, small fishes, frogs, snails, insects and many micro-organisms. Sunlight reaches the water, and the mud at the bottom is rich in minerals. The pond has been there for many years without anyone caring for it.
(a) Name the abiotic components mentioned in the passage.
(b) Is this pond a natural or an artificial ecosystem? Give a reason.
(c) Name one producer and one consumer in this pond.
(d) What kind of ecosystem (terrestrial or aquatic) is it?
questions.answer:
(a) Abiotic components: sunlight, water and minerals in the mud.
(b) It is a NATURAL ecosystem, because it has formed and runs on its own for many years without human care or inputs.
(c) Producer: water plants or algae. Consumer: small fish, frog, snail or insect (any one).
(d) It is an AQUATIC ecosystem (water-based).
questions.explanation: Tests identification of abiotic parts, natural vs artificial, biotic roles and ecosystem type.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a forest, green trees and grasses grow. Deer and rabbits feed on the grass and leaves. Tigers and leopards hunt the deer. When any plant or animal dies, bacteria and fungi in the soil break it down.
(a) Name the producers in this forest.
(b) Which animals are herbivores and which are carnivores?
(c) What is the role of the bacteria and fungi?
(d) Why are the producers important for the deer and the tiger?
questions.answer:
(a) Producers: green trees and grasses.
(b) Herbivores: deer and rabbits (they eat plants). Carnivores: tigers and leopards (they eat other animals).
(c) The bacteria and fungi are decomposers; they break down dead plants and animals into simple substances and return minerals to the soil.
(d) Producers trap the sun's energy as food. The deer eat the producers directly, and the tiger eats the deer, so both ultimately depend on the producers for energy.
questions.explanation: Tests producers, consumer types, decomposers and energy dependence.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a grassland, grass is eaten by grasshoppers. Grasshoppers are eaten by frogs, frogs by snakes, and snakes by hawks. Hawks also sometimes eat small birds that feed on grasshoppers.
(a) Write one complete food chain from this passage.
(b) Identify the producer and the top carnivore.
(c) Explain why this is described as a food web rather than a single food chain.
(d) State the trophic level of the frog.
questions.answer:
(a) Food chain: Grass -> Grasshopper -> Frog -> Snake -> Hawk.
(b) Producer: grass. Top carnivore: hawk.
(c) It is a food web because there is more than one feeding pathway — for example, hawks eat both snakes and small birds, and grasshoppers are eaten by both frogs and small birds. These interconnected chains form a web.
(d) The frog is at the third trophic level (it is a secondary consumer / carnivore that eats the herbivorous grasshopper).
questions.explanation: Tests building a chain, producer/top carnivore, food-web concept and trophic level.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a food chain, the grass (producers) stores 10000 units of energy. The energy then passes to grasshoppers, then to frogs, and then to snakes. At each step only about one-tenth of the energy is passed on.
(a) How much energy reaches the grasshoppers?
(b) How much energy reaches the snakes?
(c) What happens to the rest of the energy at each step?
(d) Use these numbers to explain why food chains are usually short.
questions.answer:
(a) Grasshoppers receive 10% of 10000 = 1000 units.
(b) Frogs receive 10% of 1000 = 100 units; snakes receive 10% of 100 = 10 units. So the snakes get about 10 units.
(c) The rest (about 90% at each step) is used up in life processes such as respiration and movement and is lost to the surroundings as heat.
(d) Because about 90% of the energy is lost at every step, very little energy is left after three or four transfers (10000 -> 1000 -> 100 -> 10). There is not enough energy to support many higher levels, so food chains are usually short (3 to 5 links).
questions.explanation: Tests application of the 10% law and reasoning about chain length.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The air contains about 78% nitrogen gas, but plants and animals cannot use this gas directly. Bacteria in the soil and in the roots of pea plants convert it into a usable form. After plants and animals die, other bacteria release the nitrogen, and some bacteria send free nitrogen back into the air.
(a) What is the process of converting atmospheric nitrogen into a usable form called?
(b) Name the bacterium found in the roots of pea (legume) plants.
(c) How do animals obtain nitrogen?
(d) Which process returns free nitrogen gas to the atmosphere?
questions.answer:
(a) The process is called nitrogen fixation.
(b) The bacterium is Rhizobium, found in the root nodules of legumes such as pea.
(c) Animals obtain nitrogen by eating plants (or by eating other animals that ate plants); they cannot use nitrogen gas directly.
(d) Denitrification (carried out by denitrifying bacteria) returns free nitrogen gas to the atmosphere.
questions.explanation: Tests the steps of the nitrogen cycle: fixation, uptake, denitrification.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
High in the atmosphere there is a layer of a gas that absorbs most of the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays. In recent decades scientists found that this layer is thinning, especially over Antarctica, because of certain chemicals used in refrigerators and sprays. In 1987 many countries agreed to ban these chemicals.
(a) Name the gas and the layer described.
(b) Why is this layer important for life?
(c) Name the chemicals responsible for thinning it.
(d) What is the thinning over Antarctica called, and what agreement banned these chemicals?
questions.answer:
(a) The gas is ozone (O3) and the layer is the ozone layer (in the stratosphere).
(b) It is important because it absorbs most of the sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation, which can cause skin cancer, cataracts and weakened immunity and can damage crops and aquatic life. It makes life on land possible.
(c) The chemicals are chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
(d) The thinning over Antarctica is called the ozone hole; the Montreal Protocol (1987) banned these chemicals.
questions.explanation: Tests the ozone layer, its importance, CFCs, the ozone hole and the Montreal Protocol.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a pond food web, phytoplankton are eaten by zooplankton; zooplankton are eaten by small fish; small fish are eaten by big fish; and big fish are also eaten by birds. Suppose a disease kills almost all the small fish.
(a) What will happen to the zooplankton population? Why?
(b) What will happen to the big fish? Why?
(c) How might the food web help the birds survive?
(d) What does this show about the stability of food webs?
questions.answer:
(a) The zooplankton population will increase, because the small fish (their predator) have died, so fewer zooplankton are eaten.
(b) The big fish will decline, because the small fish were their main food source; with little food, fewer big fish survive.
(c) If the birds can feed on other prey in the web (for example other fish or organisms), they can switch food sources and still survive — the web gives them alternatives.
(d) It shows that food webs with many interconnected links are more stable: the loss of one species can be partly absorbed because organisms have alternative food sources.
questions.explanation: Tests reasoning about disturbance propagation and food-web stability.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A region near a town once had a dense forest with many kinds of birds, animals and plants. Over the years, the forest was cleared for farms and buildings, rivers were polluted, and several animal species are no longer seen. The government now plans to set up a wildlife sanctuary nearby.
(a) What term describes the variety of living organisms that the forest had?
(b) Name two human activities in the passage that reduced this variety.
(c) Why is the loss of this variety harmful?
(d) How will a wildlife sanctuary help?
questions.answer:
(a) The term is biodiversity (biological diversity).
(b) Two activities: clearing the forest (deforestation) and polluting the rivers (also building/urbanisation).
(c) Loss of biodiversity makes ecosystems less stable and resilient, disturbs natural cycles (clean air, water, fertile soil) and reduces resources such as food and medicines; it can lead to extinction of species and upset ecological balance.
(d) A wildlife sanctuary is a protected area where animals and plants are conserved in their natural habitat, hunting and habitat destruction are controlled, and species can recover — helping to conserve biodiversity.
questions.explanation: Tests biodiversity, causes and effects of its loss, and conservation through sanctuaries.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A student set up an aquarium with water plants, a few small fish and snails. She fed the fish daily, cleaned the glass, and used a pump to keep the water aerated. After a holiday during which no one cared for it, the fish died.
(a) Name the producer and a consumer in the aquarium.
(b) Is the aquarium a natural or an artificial ecosystem?
(c) Why did the fish die when the aquarium was not cared for?
(d) What role would decomposers play in this aquarium?
questions.answer:
(a) Producer: the water plants. Consumer: the fish (or the snails).
(b) It is an artificial (man-made) ecosystem.
(c) An artificial ecosystem depends on human inputs. Without feeding, cleaning and aeration, the food and oxygen ran short and wastes built up, so the fish could not survive.
(d) Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) would break down the dead fish, leftover food and wastes into simple substances, releasing minerals back into the water for the plants to use.
questions.explanation: Tests producers/consumers, artificial-ecosystem dependence and the role of decomposers.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
An ecologist drew a figure shaped like a triangle, broad at the bottom and narrow at the top. The bottom band represented the grasses, the next the deer, and the top the tigers. She made one such figure for the energy at each level.
(a) What is such a triangular figure called?
(b) Why is the band for grasses the broadest?
(c) Will the energy figure ever be inverted? Why or why not?
(d) Name the other two kinds of such figures.
questions.answer:
(a) It is called an ecological pyramid.
(b) The grasses are producers and contain the most energy (and usually the greatest number/biomass), so their band is the broadest; energy decreases at each higher level.
(c) The energy pyramid will NEVER be inverted, because by the 10 per cent law energy always decreases as we move up the trophic levels and can never increase.
(d) The other two kinds are the pyramid of numbers and the pyramid of biomass.
questions.explanation: Tests ecological pyramids, the upright energy pyramid and the three pyramid types.
